title: The Classroom
answer: Part II, The Classroom, covers AI in each stage and subject. It begins with preschool through second grade, then turns to reading and writing, mathematics, science and computing, social studies and world languages, the arts and physical education, and personalized learning and tutoring.

children.name: Preschool Through Second Grade
children.blurb: In a 2026 study, researchers asked 310 children aged 4 to 6 where they would go to learn how something in science works. The children could choose a digital voice assistant, a classmate, or their classroom teacher.

children.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade
children.blurb: In a classroom in Finland, seventh graders were given an unusual writing partner. A program called the Poetry Machine offered each student a draft poem, and the students were free to change it however they liked.

children.name: Mathematics, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade
children.blurb: A team of researchers spent months designing an AI math tutor for fifth graders. It followed a strict set of rules: first figure out where the student was stuck, then choose what kind of help to give, then respond only in ways that fit that choice.

children.name: Science, STEM, and Computer Science
children.blurb: Before they had any lessons on the subject, 195 fifth and sixth graders in Finland were asked what artificial intelligence is. Their answers were varied and often confused.

children.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages
children.blurb: Picture a middle school class studying the abolition movement. The teacher sets up an AI tool to answer questions in the voice of Frederick Douglass, and students line up to interview him.

children.name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health
children.blurb: In a small study in Turkey, one class of sixth graders took a visual arts course that used AI tools, while a similar class took the same course without them. By the end, the students who used AI held more positive attitudes toward art and scored higher on the course outcomes (Kara, 2025).

children.name: Personalized Learning and Tutoring
children.blurb: For decades, education researchers have pointed to one on one tutoring as one of the most powerful ways to help a student learn. The problem has always been cost, since no school can afford a tutor for every child.

sections.body: This section of the book looks at how AI shows up in each stage and subject of a school, starting with the youngest learners and moving through the grades. It covers preschool through second grade, then reading and writing, mathematics, science and computing, social studies and world languages, the arts and physical education, and personalized learning and tutoring. Each chapter sorts its ideas by grade band, so a teacher can find what fits their students. The book treats the classroom as the place where AI meets real subjects and real ages, not as one general topic.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book holds that what works depends on the grade band and the subject, and it sorts its ideas by both grade band and evidence. It does not offer one answer for every classroom, and it does not treat AI as equally useful everywhere. The rule it holds to is that teachers should find their own subjects and grades in these pages and judge what fits their students. What does not work is anything applied without regard to the age or the subject in front of the teacher.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move in the same order as the section, beginning with Preschool Through Second Grade for the youngest learners and then Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade for literacy across the years. Mathematics, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade and Science, STEM, and Computer Science cover the number and inquiry subjects, while Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages and Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health cover the human and physical sides of the day. Personalized Learning and Tutoring closes the set for teachers and leaders thinking about individual support, and a parent would go to the page matching their child's subject or grade to see what the book says fits.
